grain: one row per file under sources/
what_it_answers: THE INDEX INTO THE ARCHIVE'S BYTES. Every file under `sources/` -- 25,164 of them -- with its R2 object key, its size, its sha256, the etag MD5 the bucket returns, and the publisher URL it came from where one is recorded. This is what `sync_archive.py --pull` reads to fetch the documents a fresh clone does not have, and what `check_archive_storage.py` reconciles the bucket against. It is tracked in git deliberately: a clone held only in R2 would have to ask the network what exists before it could ask for any of it.
caution: NOT A LIST OF DOCUMENTS. It is a list of FILES, and most of them are ours rather than the publishers' -- 24,033 of the 25,164 keys are under `meetings/`, which includes our extracted text, and `data/` and `analyses/` are things we wrote. Which keys are the publisher's own is not a column here: `archive_storage.frozen()` decides it from the extension and the folder, and only those are frozen in the bucket. `upstream` is empty on 12,565 rows -- an address nobody recorded, not a document with no source. `etag_md5` is the bucket's checksum for a single-part upload and is not a content hash for a multipart one; compare `sha256`.

grain: one row per object sync_archive.py --push has uploaded and read back
what_it_answers: What `--push` has already uploaded to the R2 bucket and verified, so a resumed run does not re-download 1.4 GB to rediscover it. Key, size, sha256, and the UTC timestamp at which the object was read back out of the bucket and matched.
caution: A CACHE AND A CLAIM, NOT THE BUCKET. It records what a past run believed it did. `check_archive_storage.py` asks the bucket itself and never reads this file, and that is the check to trust. `verified_at` is when we read the object back, not when the town published anything. It has 19 fewer rows than the manifest; a key absent here is a key this cache has no record of, which is not the same as an object that is missing from the bucket.

grain: one row per archived document with a publisher URL, per check
what_it_answers: IS OUR COPY STILL THE PUBLISHER'S COPY? For each document, the publisher URL was re-fetched and the bytes hashed against ours. `state` says how they compare: `identical` (316), `repackaged` (a docx/xlsx re-zipped by Google, every member identical), `resaved` and `reflowed` (a PDF whose extracted text is the same but whose bytes are not), `differs` (content actually differs -- the one to look at, 1 today), `restricted` (the host answered 2xx with a sign-in page, so nothing could be compared, 3), `unreachable` (18). Checked 2026-09-05.
caution: ONLY `differs` IS A FINDING. `repackaged`, `resaved` and `reflowed` are our instrument and the publisher's, not the town editing a document -- treating them as changes would report six false alarms. `restricted` means the request SUCCEEDED and what succeeded was a login wall; it is not evidence the document changed or did not. `checked` is a date, so every row is a claim about that day. Documents with no publisher URL are absent entirely, which is not a document that matches.

grain: one row per dataset per report edition
what_it_answers: WHERE EVERY ANNUAL-REPORT FIGURE CAME FROM -- the join from a row in one of the eighteen annual-report datasets to the report it was read out of: how many rows and which pages, the document's filename, the publisher's own label, BOTH town URLs (DocumentCenter and ArchiveCenter, because links here have died 57 in a day), the sha256 and the byte count.
caution: PROVENANCE IS NOT VERIFICATION. This says where a figure came from; it does not say the figure is right. `reconciled` and `partial` are the separate question and they are 0 on all 225 rows today -- none of these extracts is reconciled to a printed total. The generator FAILS rather than writing empty columns: this file once resolved 0 of 225 editions and exited 0, because it read one hardcoded folder the reports had moved out of, and every figure silently lost its address while the row count stayed the same. `pages` is truncated to the first 60 page numbers.

grain: one row per DESE source
what_it_answers: HOW TO FETCH EACH DESE SOURCE AGAIN NEXT YEAR. Three addresses per row and they are not interchangeable: `portal_page` is what a person opens, `api_endpoint` what a program fetches (Socrata only, blank where none exists), `publisher` the page DESE actually sends you to. Plus our local path, size and sha256, what the source `offers`, and a `refresh_note` saying what to do when the obvious route is a dead end.
caution: SIX OF THE 29 ROWS ARE `source_kind = WANTED` -- a source we have identified and DO NOT HOLD. They carry no sha256 and no local file, and counting rows as documents overstates the archive by six. `archive-manifest.csv` records what we HOLD; this records how to get it again, and only one of those questions survives a year. The file format is part of the address: the Chapter 70 workbooks are VLOOKUP interfaces whose front sheet reads as empty, which is recorded per row.

grain: one row per document
what_it_answers: WHAT PRODUCED EACH DOCUMENT’S FIGURES -- rule 13a’s registry. Whether a figure came off the accounting system or was assembled by a person, plus, for every workbook, the columns the publisher HID.
caution: This is the table that decides how much weight a figure carries, and it does not look at file extensions: a MUNIS .xlsx is a printout of the books and a hand-built .xlsx is an argument. `hidden_columns` exists because two copies of the same workbook hide different sets, so "the workbook contains FY23 actuals" and "there is no FY23 column" were both true at once.

grain: one row per archived document link, per check
what_it_answers: DOES THE PUBLISHER'S OWN LINK STILL OPEN? One HTTP request per document, no concurrency, a real user agent. `code` is the status returned and `public` is 1 where it opened without a sign-in wall. 330 of 351 opened on 2026-09-05; 18 returned code `000` (the request did not complete) and 3 returned 401. Nearly every historic failure has been a Google Drive or Docs link.
caution: WHETHER A LINK OPENS IS NOT WHETHER IT HANDS BACK THE SAME DOCUMENT -- that is `copy-status.csv`, and a link can open and serve different bytes. A 200 can also BE the failure: a Google sign-in page answers 200, which is why `public` is recorded separately from `code`. `checked` is a date and this is run occasionally, never in the build, so every row is a claim about that day. `stars` and `section` come from the sources index and describe how the document is presented on the site, not its authority.

grain: one row per meeting occasion (board and date)
what_it_answers: Every meeting occasion the town held, joining its agenda, its minutes, its video and its transcript -- so a question like "was there a meeting with no minutes" is answerable in one place.
caution: An occasion with no minutes is not established to be a meeting that did not happen, nor one whose minutes are withheld: the town publishes on its own schedule and this is a snapshot. `evidence` says what the row rests on.

grain: one row per newly observed agenda or minutes document
what_it_answers: WHAT HAS APPEARED on the town's AgendaCenter since the last crawl -- the announcement feed. Board, meeting date, whether it is an agenda or minutes, the town's own file id and URL, and `first_seen`, the day our crawler first saw it.
caution: AN OBSERVATION LOG, NOT A MEASUREMENT. `first_seen` is the day WE SAW IT, never the day the town posted it -- the AgendaCenter publishes no posting timestamp. That is why the gap between the meeting date and `first_seen` is named `days_after_meeting_upper_bound`: it is an upper bound on how long minutes took to appear, and it is empty on rows carried in by `--seed`, because we genuinely do not know. Six rows today, all from the first live run on 2026-09-08; this file starts empty by design and is not a history of the archive.

grain: one row per watch run per day
what_it_answers: THE CRAWL LOG for `watch_meetings.py`: when it ran, whether it was a `live` crawl or the `seed`, how many boards and documents the town listed, how many boards did not answer, and how many new agendas and minutes it announced.
caution: `boards_unanswered` IS THE DENOMINATOR THAT MATTERS -- a run that saw fewer boards found fewer new documents for a reason that has nothing to do with the town. A second run on the same day REWRITES that day's row rather than appending, so this is one row per day, not one per invocation, and the row count is not a count of runs. `documents_listed` is what the town's listing showed, not what we hold.

grain: one row per (board, date, kind, town file id)
what_it_answers: THE WATCHER'S MEMORY -- every agenda and minutes document the town has listed that we already know about, so nothing is ever announced twice. 12,071 rows, 7,411 agendas and 4,660 sets of minutes. Identity is the town's own file id, not a path, not a hash, and not a position in a listing.
caution: `basis` SPLITS THIS FILE IN TWO AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT KINDS OF ROW. 12,065 rows are `seed` -- adopted from what we already held, announcing nothing, and carrying NO `first_seen`, because the day we first saw them is genuinely unknown. Only 6 are `observed`. Reading `first_seen` across the file measures the watcher's own start date, not the town's publishing. This is a record of what the AgendaCenter LISTED, not of what we hold or of meetings held.

grain: one row per board per year
what_it_answers: HOW MUCH OF THE TOWN'S DECISION-MAKING IS ON THE RECORD -- per board per year, how many agendas the town posted and how many sets of minutes, with the ratio. This is the coverage figure every rule 15a search must quote: a grep that finds nothing prints nothing, and nothing reads as 'nobody said it' when it means nobody said it in the record that exists.
caution: THE DENOMINATOR IS AGENDAS POSTED, NOT MEETINGS HELD, and nothing published reconciles the two -- a meeting can be held with no agenda posted, and an agenda posted for a meeting later cancelled. Say 'minutes against agendas'; calling it 'minutes against meetings held' is a proxy quoted as the thing. `basis` splits the rows: 503 are `town listing` (crawled from the town's own AgendaCenter, the authority on what exists) and 514 are `held` (recomputed offline from what WE hold, a narrower question). Do not sum across the two. And this counts documents, not what is READABLE -- `minutes-searchable.csv` is the denominator for a text search.

grain: one row per board per year
what_it_answers: How much of the meeting archive can actually be READ, per board per year -- listed, held, with a text file, searchable, and why each unsearchable document is unsearchable (image scan, vector outlines, blank, extract failed, not fetched). This is the denominator every rule 15a search must quote.
caution: A grep that finds nothing prints nothing, and nothing reads as "nobody said it". It means nobody said it IN THE DOCUMENTS THAT CAN BE READ. `searchable` is the only honest denominator; `listed` and `held` are larger and mean different things.

grain: one row per figure stated in public by a named person on a date
what_it_answers: Figures officials stated publicly, with the quote and the document -- so a number argued at a meeting can be set beside what the data produces.
caution: A figure stated is evidence of what was SAID, never of what is true. `supersedes` records where a later statement replaced an earlier one.

grain: one row per public body named in the video titles
what_it_answers: THE BOARD REGISTRY behind the video classification: the 40 bodies whose names appear in PEG-channel titles, each with the AgendaCenter folder it maps to, what kind of body it is (33 town, 3 school, 2 state, 1 district, 1 federal), every spelling seen in a title, and `basis` -- the argument that those spellings are one body. Where to look before assuming 'Selectmen' and 'Select Board' are two boards.
caution: `names_seen_in_titles` IS A LIST OF SPELLINGS, INCLUDING TYPOS ('Selec tBoard', 'Fnance Committe Meeting'), because titles are stored verbatim. `basis` is OUR argument that a set of spellings is one body -- it is judgement, recorded so it can be disputed, not something the town published. `meetings_folder` can be empty for a body with no AgendaCenter folder (Town Meeting, for one), which is not a body that does not exist.
generator: scripts/build_youtube_classification.py (registry maintained by hand; the classifier asserts every board it names exists here)

grain: one row per human correction to a video classification
what_it_answers: HUMAN CORRECTIONS to the video classification, keyed on video id, with who corrected it, when, and why. It is READ by the classifier and NEVER WRITTEN by it, so an improvement to the classification cannot silently discard a correction somebody made. The count applied is printed on every run, including when it is zero.
caution: EMPTY TODAY -- 0 rows. That is nobody having corrected anything yet, not a classification confirmed correct. A row here OVERRIDES the model's reading for that video and nothing re-derives it, so a correction that later stops being right will keep being applied until somebody removes it.

grain: one row per distinct video title stem
what_it_answers: OUR READING OF EACH VIDEO TITLE -- one row per distinct title stem (the title with the date stripped), saying whether it is a `meeting` (298), `not_a_meeting` (1,282) or `undetermined` (14), which boards it names, and a category. This is where the judgement lives, so improving it never means re-fetching anything from the channel.
caution: A JUDGEMENT ABOUT A STRING, NEVER THE CHANNEL'S OWN LABEL. `undetermined` is a real and deliberate outcome -- a title we could not read -- and it must not be folded into either of the others; the alternative to representing something correctly is recording that we could not. `not_a_meeting` is a positive finding, not a leftover: the channel's sixth commonest stem is `St. Boniface Mass`. `boards` can hold SEVERAL boards for a tri-board meeting; the per-video board rows are in `youtube-video-boards.csv`. Row count is TITLE STEMS, not videos.
generator: hand-classified; read and asserted by scripts/build_youtube_classification.py

grain: one row per video whose captions were fetched
what_it_answers: WHICH MEETING RECORDINGS HAVE A TRANSCRIPT -- the video id, the board, the meeting date, the path to the caption JSON under `sources/data/youtube-transcripts/`, how many segments and seconds it covers, the language, whether the captions were auto-generated, and when they were fetched.
caution: A TRANSCRIPT IS A FINDING AID AND NEVER A SOURCE. An auto-generated caption is a machine's rendering of audio and it mangles exactly what this project cares about -- 'fifteen hundred', '$1,500' and '$50' are the same sound to a caption model. Quote the video at that timestamp, or the document the transcript points you to; never a figure off a caption. `generated = auto` marks captions nobody typed. Barely populated and actively growing, so the row count in this registry lags the file: a video absent from the index is one nobody has fetched yet, not one with no captions.

grain: one row per (video, board) pair
what_it_answers: WHICH BOARD EACH MEETING RECORDING IS OF -- one row per video per board, so a tri-board meeting is three rows rather than a `board_2` column. Carries the board slug and name, the title stem it was read from, the AgendaCenter folder, whether that board is in the AgendaCenter at all, the meeting date, and who classified it and when.
caution: ONE VIDEO CAN HAVE SEVERAL ROWS, so counting rows counts board-appearances and not meetings -- 2,873 rows against 2,857 videos classified as meetings. The board is OUR reading of a title (`classification_source`, `classified_by`), not something the channel published. `meeting_date` is read out of the title, which is the day the meeting was held rather than the day the recording was posted; a video whose title carries no date has none here.

grain: one row per video
what_it_answers: WHAT EACH PEG-CHANNEL VIDEO IS -- all 4,671 videos with our reading applied: `meeting` (2,857), `not_a_meeting` (1,800) or `undetermined` (14), the category, how many boards it names, the meeting date and where that date was read from (`date_source`), plus the title verbatim and the URL. The bridge between the raw channel index and the board-level rows.
caution: EVERY COLUMN AFTER `url` IS OURS, and `title` is the channel's, verbatim, typos included. `meeting_date` is derived from the title -- `date_source` says how -- and 2 rows carry a `date_flag` saying the date falls after the index date and the title may carry a typo. A recording is not minutes: it is an account of a meeting, and the town posted minutes for a fraction of the meetings it held, which is why this exists. `undetermined` must stay its own outcome and never be squeezed into the nearest slot.

grain: one row per video the channel published
what_it_answers: THE PEG CHANNEL'S VIDEO INDEX, as close to what the channel published as we can get: video id, the title EXACTLY as posted, the URL, duration in seconds, view count, and `channel_rank` -- the channel's own ordering, 0 = newest. No classification and no board: what a video is for is a judgement about a string and it is made in `youtube-title-classification.csv` instead.
caution: `uploaded` IS EMPTY ON ALL 4,671 ROWS -- a flat extraction returns no upload date, so `channel_rank` is the only chronology this file has, and sorting by `uploaded` sorts by nothing. The dates ARE in the titles and are read out in the classification files, where they are the day the meeting was HELD rather than the day somebody posted the recording; the two are not the same and this column is named for the second. Titles are verbatim -- not stripped, not normalised, not title-cased. THE RECORDINGS THEMSELVES ARE NOT ARCHIVED and never will be: this is an index, and a link to somebody else's platform is not a copy.
